newsitem.title: USA: Commerce chief sees defeat of China MFN challenge.
newsitem.headline: Commerce chief sees defeat of China MFN challenge.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of Commerce William Daley said on Friday he believes the House of Representatives will reject efforts to end normal U.S. trade relations with China.

He said he expects a tough fight between trade advocates and lawmakers who want to deny Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trade status with China because of concerns about human rights abuses, nuclear technology transfers and the future of Hong Kong after the British colony comes under Chinese rule on July 1. The $38 billion U.S. trade deficit with China last year is also weighing on lawmakers.

But Daley said efforts by President Bill Clinton and other administration officials as well as the business community to explain why they feel the United States should remain engaged with China are beginning to pay off.

"I think we are in good shape right now," Daley said in an interview. A resolution against China's MFN status will be defeated, he predicted. A string of administration officials as well as Clinton have spoken in recent days of the dangers to both U.S. security and commercial interests if MFN is revoked.
Clinton on Thursday urged a group of business executives to tell members of Congress in both parties that "this is not about whether we agree with China on every issue.
"It is about what is in the interests of the American people and what is most likely to give us the largest amount of influence and cooperation with China in the years ahead," he said.

Business leaders have been rallying commercial forces across the country since January to lobby lawmakers for renewal of the trade status that is given just about every other country in the world. Only a handful of countries are denied MFN status.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told Congress this week that ending China's MFN status would send import duties on Chinese goods soaring to an average 44 percent, compared to about six percent currenty.
She said Americans would end up paying about $590 million more a year for goods such as shoes, clothing and small appliances.

The House Ways and Means Committee is expected to hold a hearing next week on China MFN and vote on a resolution that would deny the trade privilege to Beijing. A committee aide said the panel is expected to send the measure to the full House for action later this month with a recommendation that their fellow lawmakers vote against it.

Last year the House upheld the president's decision to renew MFN by a comfortable 286-141 margin. The Senate never took up the issue. Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich has said he expects a closer vote this year.
Efforts in Congress to overturn the president on MFN have been unsuccessful since the 1989 Chinese army crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square.
